meta.subject: maths
meta.title: Triangles
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 6 (jemh106.pdf, printed pages 73-98)

board_asks: the three similarity criteria (AAA/AA, SSS, SAS), the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales) and its converse, and similar-triangle applications (heights, shadows, distances) - plus the ONE proof CBSE can ask you to write here: Theorem 6.1 (BPT). The rationalised 2026-27 chapter stops at the SAS criterion - areas of similar triangles and the Pythagoras proofs are no longer in this chapter.

big_idea.body: Two figures are similar when they have the same shape but not necessarily the same size - one is a scaled copy of the other. For triangles this means equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. The chapter gives you shortcuts (the AAA, SSS and SAS criteria) to decide similarity from just three facts, the Basic Proportionality Theorem to split sides in ratio, and a way to measure the unmeasurable - heights of towers and lengths of shadows - by comparing similar triangles.

definitions.verbatim: Two figures having the same shape but not necessarily the same size are called similar figures.
definitions.plain: same shape, any size. Every pair of congruent figures is automatically similar, but similar figures need not be congruent (a small photo and its enlargement are similar, not congruent).

definitions.verbatim: Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
definitions.plain: for polygons you need BOTH conditions: every corresponding angle equal AND every corresponding side in the same ratio. Either one alone is not enough (a square and a rectangle share angles but not ratios; a square and a rhombus share ratios but not angles).

definitions.verbatim: Two triangles are similar, if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion).
definitions.plain: the same two conditions as polygons - but for triangles, verifying ONE of them automatically forces the other. That is exactly what the AAA/SSS/SAS criteria below exploit, so you never have to check all six pairs.

source.note: restated at the head of Section 6.4; the same statement first appears in Section 6.3 (p.79)

definitions.verbatim: Theorem 6.1 : If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
definitions.plain: the Thales Theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally, $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{AE}{EC}$. This is the ONE theorem in this chapter CBSE can ask you to PROVE - see the Proof tab.

definitions.verbatim: Theorem 6.3 : If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportion) and hence the two triangles are similar.
definitions.plain: equal angles $\Rightarrow$ proportional sides $\Rightarrow$ similar. Since a triangle's third angle is fixed once two are known, two equal pairs of angles are already enough - that shorter form is the AA criterion.

definitions.verbatim: Theorem 6.5 : If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.
definitions.plain: one equal angle that sits BETWEEN two pairs of sides in the same ratio $\Rightarrow$ similar. The equal angle must be the included angle - the one between the two proportional sides.

definitions.verbatim: Note that the same ratio of the corresponding sides is referred to as the scale factor (or the Representative Fraction) for the polygons.
Theorem 6.2 : If a line divides any two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side.
If in two triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio, then their corresponding angles are equal and hence the triangles are similar.

source.note: Summary point 8 (SSS criterion); the same result is Theorem 6.4, p.88

definitions.verbatim: If two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.

concepts.title: Similar vs congruent - same shape, any size
concepts.body: Congruent figures match in shape AND size; similar figures match in shape only. So all congruent figures are similar, but the converse is not true. All circles are similar, all squares are similar, all equilateral triangles are similar - because their shape is fixed.

concepts.title: The two similarity conditions (and why triangles are special)
concepts.body: For any pair of polygons, similarity needs BOTH equal corresponding angles AND proportional corresponding sides. For triangles only, one condition automatically brings the other - which is why the three criteria each need just three facts. When you write the similarity, match vertices in order: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ means $\angle A=\angle D$, $\angle B=\angle E$, $\angle C=\angle F$.
concepts.tested: State the criterion + write the similarity in correct vertex order (Exercise 6.3 Q1)

concepts.title: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales) and its converse
concepts.body: BPT (Theorem 6.1): a line parallel to one side divides the other two sides in the same ratio, $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{AE}{EC}$. Its converse (Theorem 6.2) runs backwards: if a line divides two sides in the same ratio, it must be parallel to the third side. Use BPT to find a missing length; use the converse to prove two lines parallel.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark find EC/AD when DE || BC; prove a line is parallel (Exercise 6.2)

concepts.title: Picking a criterion - AAA/AA, SSS, SAS
concepts.body: AA: two pairs of equal angles. SSS: all three pairs of sides in the same ratio. SAS: one pair of equal angles with the two including sides in the same ratio. Scan the figure for what you are given - equal angles (from parallels, vertically opposite, or common angles) point to AA; three known side-ratios point to SSS.
concepts.tested: State which pairs of triangles are similar and name the criterion (Exercise 6.3 Q1)

concepts.title: Measuring the unmeasurable - heights, shadows, distances
concepts.body: Similar triangles let you find a height or distance you cannot reach: set up two triangles that share equal angles (usually AA - a common angle plus two right angles), then equate a pair of corresponding sides and solve. This is the principle behind finding heights of towers, lengths of shadows, and even distances of far-off objects.
concepts.tested: 3-4 mark height-of-tower / length-of-shadow word problem (Example 7, Exercise 6.3 Q15)

examples.problem_verbatim: If a line intersects sides AB and AC of a △ABC at D and E respectively and is parallel to BC, prove that AD/AB = AE/AC (see Fig. 6.13).

solution_steps.lead: Apply BPT to the given parallel line.
Take reciprocals and add 1 to both sides.
solution_steps.concept_tag: convert DB, EC into whole sides AB, AC

solution_steps.lead: Invert to reach the required result.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark proof: 1 for invoking Theorem 6.1 (BPT) on the parallel line, 1 for the reciprocal-and-add-1 step that turns DB and EC into the full sides AB and AC, 1 for inverting to the stated result.

examples.shape: Converse of BPT -> isosceles - NCERT Example 3
examples.problem_verbatim: In Fig. 6.16, PS/SQ = PT/TR and ∠PST = ∠PRQ. Prove that PQR is an isosceles triangle.

solution_steps.text: Given $\dfrac{PS}{SQ}=\dfrac{PT}{TR}$, so by Theorem 6.2 (converse of BPT), $ST \parallel QR$.
solution_steps.concept_tag: converse of BPT gives a parallel

solution_steps.text: $ST \parallel QR \Rightarrow \angle PST=\angle PQR$ (corresponding angles) $\;\ldots(1)$. It is also given that $\angle PST=\angle PRQ \;\ldots(2)$.
From (1) and (2), $\angle PRQ=\angle PQR$, so $PQ=PR$ (sides opposite equal angles). Hence $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark proof: 1 for using the converse of BPT (Theorem 6.2) to get ST || QR, 1 for combining the two corresponding-angle facts, 1 for concluding PQ = PR (isosceles). Skipping the 'sides opposite equal angles' reason is the usual lost mark.

source.note: problem on p.83, solution completes on p.84

examples.shape: AAA similarity via parallels - NCERT Example 4
examples.problem_verbatim: In Fig. 6.29, if PQ || RS, prove that △POQ ~ △SOR.

solution_steps.lead: Parallels give two pairs of equal angles.
solution_steps.text: $PQ \parallel RS \Rightarrow \angle P=\angle S$ and $\angle Q=\angle R$ (alternate angles).

solution_steps.lead: Add the vertical angle and conclude.
solution_steps.text: $\angle POQ=\angle SOR$ (vertically opposite angles), so all three angle pairs are equal; hence $\triangle POQ \sim \triangle SOR$ by the AAA similarity criterion.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark proof: 1 for the two pairs of equal alternate angles, 1 for adding the vertically-opposite angle and quoting the AAA similarity criterion with the vertices in correct order.

examples.problem_verbatim: A girl of height 90 cm is walking away from the base of a lamp-post at a speed of 1.2 m/s. If the lamp is 3.6 m above the ground, find the length of her shadow after 4 seconds.

solution_steps.text: Let $AB$ be the lamp-post and $CD$ the girl after 4 s; let her shadow $DE=x$ m. She has walked $BD=1.2 \times 4=4.8$ m.
In $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CDE$: $\angle B=\angle D$ (each $90°$, both stand vertical) and $\angle E=\angle E$ (common). So $\triangle ABE \sim \triangle CDE$ (AA similarity).
$4.8+x=4x \Rightarrow 3x=4.8 \Rightarrow x=1.6$. The shadow is $1.6$ m long.

examples.mark_logic: 4-mark application: 1 for modelling (naming x, computing BD = 4.8 m), 1 for the AA similarity, 1 for equating corresponding sides into an equation, 1 for solving to x = 1.6 m with the unit. Dropping the unit costs 0.5 by the CBSE scheme.

source.note: problem on p.92, solution completes on p.93

strategies.text: Hunt for equal angles first (from parallels, vertically opposite, or a common angle) -> AA. No angles? Check if all three side pairs share a ratio -> SSS. One angle plus its two including sides in ratio -> SAS.

strategies.cue: Need to PROVE two lines parallel?
strategies.text: Show the line divides two sides of the triangle in the same ratio, then quote Theorem 6.2 (converse of BPT).

strategies.cue: A line is drawn parallel to a side?
strategies.text: Quote Theorem 6.1 (BPT) at once: it splits the other two sides in the same ratio.

strategies.cue: Height / shadow / distance you cannot measure?
strategies.text: Build two similar triangles (usually AA - a common angle and two right angles), then equate a pair of corresponding sides and solve.
Match vertices in order. $\angle A=\angle D$ forces $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ - never $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EDF$. The ratio chain follows the same order.

pitfalls.text: Wrong vertex order in the similarity - writing $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle EDF$ instead of $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ breaks every ratio and angle that follows.

Assuming one condition is enough for polygons - a square and a rectangle have equal angles but not equal ratios; a square and a rhombus have equal ratios but not equal angles. Only for TRIANGLES does one condition imply the other.
Confusing BPT with its converse - Theorem 6.1 needs the line GIVEN parallel and concludes a ratio; Theorem 6.2 needs the ratio GIVEN equal and concludes parallel. Quote the right direction.
Pairing the wrong sides in the ratio - after $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$, the ratio is $\frac{AB}{DE}=\frac{BC}{EF}=\frac{CA}{FD}$, not $\frac{AB}{EF}$. Follow the vertex correspondence.
In SAS, using a non-included angle - the equal angle must sit BETWEEN the two proportional sides, or SAS does not apply.

third_tab_content.name: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Theorem 6.1) - the area proof
third_tab_content.intro: In the rationalised 2026-27 syllabus, BPT (Theorem 6.1) is the one theorem in this chapter marked '(Prove)' - its formal proof is examinable. The three criteria (AAA/SSS/SAS) and the converse are '(Motivate)' - you must know the statements but are not asked for their formal proofs. Below is NCERT's area-ratio proof of BPT.

steps.claim: Given: $\triangle ABC$ with a line $DE \parallel BC$ meeting $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$. To prove that the two sides are divided in the same ratio.
Join $BE$ and $CD$, and drop perpendiculars $DM \perp AC$ and $EN \perp AB$ to serve as the heights.
Write the areas of the two triangles on base $AD$ and $DB$ (common height $EN$).
Likewise for the two triangles on base $AE$ and $EC$ (common height $DM$).
Divide each pair - the common heights cancel, leaving the side ratios.
$\triangle BDE$ and $\triangle DEC$ sit on the same base $DE$ and between the same parallels $BC$ and $DE$, so they have equal area.
steps.justification: Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area (Class IX result).

steps.claim: From (1), (2) and (3): the numerators are the same $\text{ar}(ADE)$ and the denominators are equal, so the two ratios are equal.
steps.justification: This proves BPT; the converse (Theorem 6.2) is obtained by running the argument backwards.
